newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Rocard sees rise in capital gains tax.
newsitem.headline: France's Rocard sees rise in capital gains tax.

text.p: Former French Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard said on Thursday he believed the party would boost capital gains taxes to help fund its economic programme.

"We probably will be led initially to raise taxes on capital gains...We want to increase them to the European average," said Rocard, who led the party to a disastrous defeat in 1993 and is not seen as an official who speaks for the party line.
"We think we could get from that the room to breathe," he said.
Party leader Lionel Jospin has pledged not to raise income taxes and payroll charges.
Rocard said this money, which he estimated at 10 to 20 billion francs, would help fill the shortfall created by the party's decision not to privatise France Telecom.
Analysts had forecast the treasury could raise nearly 50 billion francs from the privatisation.
The ruling centre-right coalition, defeated by the left in the first round last Sunday of France's parliamentary election, put the privatisation on hold for the election.
The final vote will be held this Sunday.
The money to be raised from the France Telecom sale was earmarked by the centre-right for recapitalising state companies suffering financial difficulties in order to sell them.
He also said the Socialists were counting on savings from the health care insurance system to finance its programme whose centrepiece is a plan to create 700,000 jobs.

Rocard cited an official report suggesting there were 80 to 100 billion francs of wasted expenditure in the health sector. "Naturally, you can't do it (make the savings) all in one year, it will be a long procedure," he said.
He suggested implementing reforms to eliminate multiple medical exams and use of generic instead of brand name drugs.
He said under five percent of drugs used in France were generic. "For us that's where the biggest savings lie," he said.

Rocard said international financial markets had nothing to fear from a Socialist victory. "We will maintain the same serious sense of rigour," he said, adding that the Socialists' financial and fiscal plans were at the "cutting edge".

He defended the party's call for flexibility in interpreting the Maastricht criteria on monetary union, saying Germany's difficulties in meeting the strict conditions should make it more open to dialogue.
He reiterated the Socialists' view that Italy should be included in the first wave of monetary union even if it does not meet the Maastricht conditions exactly.
-- Paris Newsroom + Jean-Michel Belot and William Emmanuel
